    Summary and Schedule

    This is a free, open companion to the ADCI microcredential on human factors in cyber security and privacy. It is not an official Carpentries lesson. It uses the open Carpentries Workbench format so that anyone can read it, teach from it or adapt it.

    You do not need to be enrolled in the microcredential to use it. You also do not need any technical background. Across twelve short episodes you will look at the people side of security: how attackers persuade, how identity and trust work, why insiders matter, how privacy law protects personal information, and what good security awareness looks like at work.

    Who this lesson is for

    • Employees and volunteers in small organisations who handle other people’s information.
    • Managers who need to make sensible, low-cost security and privacy decisions.
    • Educators and trainers who want open material they can teach from or reuse.
    • Learners in the microcredential who want extra practice.

    How it relates to the microcredential

    The microcredential is a separate course run by ADCI. This lesson covers the same themes in a more practical, self-contained way, with its own activities and examples. Completing this lesson does not replace the microcredential. Each episode ends with a short note on where the topic appears in the microcredential, for anyone who wants the credential.

    How to use it

    On your own. Work through the episodes in order. Each takes about 45 to 60 minutes, including the activities. Try each challenge before you open the solution.

    With a group. Each episode has instructor notes, which appear inline in Instructor View, and there is an instructor notes page with general advice. It is built for a single session, in person or online. Use the discussion prompts to bring in your own workplace examples.

    Objectives are tagged ULO 1, 2 or 3, the three unit learning outcomes of SEC101 and the microcredential: ULO 1 is to analyse and respond to complex impacts on humans at the individual, group and organisational level, ULO 2 is to provide solutions to information and cyber issues in a personal or organisational setting and communicate the findings, and ULO 3 is to analyse privacy issues when working with digital systems and provide ethical and practical solutions.

    Every episode follows the same pattern: questions and objectives, short teaching sections, two activities, a quick check, ideas to go deeper, a pointer to the credential, and a reference list.

    The example organisation

    Many activities use Riverbend Community Library, a fictional small organisation. It is described on the learner pages so that every activity starts from the same facts.

    Setup Instructions Download files required for the lesson
    Duration: 00h 00m  1. Digital lives: why we protect data and systems How have digital networks changed life for individuals, groups and organisations?
    Why do we protect data and systems, and what happens when we fail?
    Why do attackers so often target people instead of technology?
    Duration: 00h 55m  2. Social engineering: hacking the human What is social engineering, and why does it work on sensible people?
    What are the main tactics, and how do you tell them apart?
    How does an attack unfold, and what helps you stop one?
    Duration: 01h 50m  3. Identity, identity management and identity theft What is an identity online, and how does identity theft happen?
    How does an organisation decide who can open what?
    How does one stolen identity harm individuals, groups and organisations?
    Duration: 02h 45m  4. The insider threat Who is an insider, and why are insiders such a difficult problem?
    How do malicious, negligent and compromised insiders differ, and what control suits each?
    What is espionage, and why do organisations take it seriously?
    Duration: 03h 40m  5. Attack techniques and human defences How do attackers get in through direct access, identity theft, phishing and social engineering?
    Which human defence best answers each technique?
    Why do espionage and insider approaches depend on people as much as on technology?
    Duration: 04h 35m  6. Privacy and privacy impact assessments What is information privacy, what harms follow when it fails, and who is responsible for it?
    What makes a response to a privacy problem both ethical and practical?
    What is a privacy impact assessment, and how does a quick threshold assessment decide whether a project needs one?
    Duration: 05h 33m  7. Social media and what attackers can build from it How can a public social media profile be joined up and used against its owner?
    How does social software lead to fake accounts, hijacked accounts and personal attacks?
    What can you do to share what you want while giving away less?
    Duration: 06h 28m  8. People at work: BYOD and working from home How should an organisation manage people, including unhappy staff, social media use and its own control over staff?
    What does a security rule gain, and what does it cost the people who must follow it?
    What are the risks and sensible controls for staff using their own devices, or working away from the office?
    Duration: 07h 23m  9. Security awareness that changes behaviour What makes a security awareness activity change what people do, and not just what they have heard?
    How can an organisation check that behaviour has really changed?
    How secure is your own ICT life, and what is one change you can make this week?
    Duration: 08h 18m 10. Vetting, trust and access What can vetting tell an organisation about a person, and what can it not tell?
    Why is vetting only one layer of protection?
    How can compartmentalisation limit what any one person can reach or know, and what does it cost the people who work under it?
    Duration: 09h 13m 11. Australian privacy law and data breaches Who does the Privacy Act cover, and which Australian Privacy Principle fits a given privacy problem?
    What must an organisation do when it suspects a data breach?
    What did the 2024 changes and the Cyber Security Act 2024 add?
    Duration: 10h 08m 12. Responding to identity theft, and what comes next In what order should a person respond when their identity is stolen, and why does the order matter?
    How might cybercrime, cyber war, connected devices, big data and quantum computing change people’s lives?
    Who is in charge of the internet, and what can you do about your own part of it?
    Duration: 11h 03m Finish

    The actual schedule may vary slightly depending on the topics and exercises chosen by the instructor.

    There is nothing to install for this lesson.

    What you need

    • A web browser, to read the episodes.
    • A notebook or a blank document, to write down your answers to the activities.
    • About 45 to 60 minutes for each episode. The episodes are short and stand on their own, so you can do one at a time.

    If you are teaching it

    You can run any episode in person or online with the same materials. Instructors will find a plan and notes for each episode on the instructor pages. A shared whiteboard or a flip chart is useful for the discussion prompts, but it is not required.

    Before you start

    Think of one small organisation you know well, such as a workplace, a club or a community group. Several activities ask you to compare the example organisation with your own.
